methods.title: Interpret the confidence level
methods.trigger: A question asks what 95% confidence means or what an interval estimates.

methods.title: Two independent means → pooled t interval
methods.trigger: Two independent groups have means, SDs, and sample sizes; estimate their population mean difference.

methods.title: One population mean → one-sample t interval
methods.trigger: One group has a sample mean, sample SD, and sample size; estimate the population mean.

methods.title: Two event proportions → course pooled z interval
methods.trigger: Two independent groups each have event counts and totals; estimate the difference in event probability.

methods.title: One event proportion → Normal interval
methods.trigger: One sample supplies an event count and total; estimate its population proportion.
formula: \hat p=\frac mn,\quad s_{\hat p}=\sqrt{\frac{\hat p(1-\hat p)}n}

methods.title: Use the interval to make a two-sided decision
methods.trigger: A confidence interval is given and the question asks whether the null population value is supported.

cases.title: BME423 student heart rate
cases.context: A sample of ten BME423 students has the heart-rate summary below. Construct a 95% interval for the population mean heart rate. Treat the sample as independent observations from a Normal population.
tasks: Construct a 95% confidence interval for the population mean. Show the standard error, degrees of freedom, critical value, margin, and both endpoints.
Interpret the interval in the measurement units and distinguish it from individual variation.
cases.symbols: \(\bar x\) (sample mean), \(s\) (sample SD), \(n\) (number sampled), \(s_{\bar x}\) (standard error of the mean), \(\mu\) (population mean), \(M\) (margin).

steps.title: Identify the population quantity
steps.words: The sample mean estimates the population mean. The SD describes individual measurements; the standard error describes uncertainty in their mean.

steps.title: Calculate the standard error
steps.words: Divide the sample SD by the square root of sample size. Keep the standard error available for the margin calculation.

steps.title: Choose degrees of freedom and the cutoff
steps.words: Open t_table.pdf, PDF page 1. Use row 9 and the combined two-tail 0.05 column. The printed cutoff is 2.262. Do not halve the column probability again.

steps.title: Calculate the margin of error
steps.words: The margin has the same measurement units as the sample mean.

steps.title: Calculate the lower endpoint
steps.words: Subtract the margin from the sample mean.

steps.title: Calculate the upper endpoint
steps.words: Add the same margin to the sample mean.

steps.title: State the population interval
steps.words: The 95% interval estimates the population mean in the original measurement units. It is not an interval containing this percentage of individual measurements.

cases.conclusion: The 95% confidence interval for the population mean is 60.56224 to 73.43776 beats/min.

cases.title: Diuretic versus placebo urine production
cases.context: A study compares daily urine production with a diuretic and a placebo. Assume independent Normal responses with a common population variance.
tasks: Construct the 95% confidence interval for the population difference, diuretic minus placebo. Show both variance contributions, the pooled variance, SE, df, critical value, margin, and both bounds.
Using the interval alone, decide whether the means differ at the matching two-sided 0.05 level. State both hypotheses in symbols and words, and conclude in context.

hypotheses.nullWords: The diuretic and placebo populations have equal means.
hypotheses.alternativeWords: The diuretic and placebo population means differ.

cases.symbols: \(\bar x_i\) (group sample mean), \(s_i\) (group sample SD), \(n_i\) (group sample size), \(s^2\) (pooled variance), \(s_d\) (SE of the difference), \(d\) (sample difference), \(\Delta\) (population difference).

steps.title: Define the contrast and hypotheses
steps.words: Keep the direction diuretic minus placebo throughout. The null means equal population means; the two-sided alternative means different population means.

steps.title: Calculate the observed difference
steps.words: This is the sample estimate of the population difference in mL/day.

steps.title: Square both group SDs
steps.words: Each SD is squared before pooling, giving variances in squared measurement units.

steps.title: Pool both variance contributions
steps.words: Weight each group variance by its own degrees of freedom, add the contributions, and divide by the combined degrees of freedom.

steps.title: Calculate the SE of the difference
steps.words: Add the two mean-variance contributions inside the root, then take the root. This restores the original measurement units.

steps.title: Find degrees of freedom and the t cutoff
steps.words: Open t_table.pdf, PDF page 1. Use row 18 and the combined two-tail 0.05 column. The printed cutoff is 2.101. Do not halve the column probability again.

steps.title: Calculate the margin
steps.words: Multiply the positive cutoff by the standard error of the difference.

steps.title: Calculate both bounds
steps.words: The bounds retain the diuretic minus placebo subtraction order.

steps.title: Make the decision using the interval
steps.words: Zero is outside the interval. Reject the equal-means null at the matching two-sided 0.05 level; no separate t statistic is required.

cases.conclusion: The 95% CI for diuretic minus placebo is 31.18917 to 408.8108 mL/day. The population means differ, with diuretic higher.

cases.title: Aspirin thrombosis interval · slide rounding
cases.context: A trial compares thrombosis incidence with placebo and aspirin. Reproduce the slide’s displayed proportions 0.72 and 0.32 and its rounded SE of 0.15.
tasks: Construct the 95% confidence interval for the difference in population event proportions using the Session 17 pooled standard error. Show both sample proportions, the pooled estimate, variance, SE, margin, and endpoints.
Use the interval to decide whether the event probabilities differ at the matching two-sided 0.05 level. Interpret the direction and distinguish percentage points from a relative reduction.

hypotheses.nullWords: The placebo and aspirin populations have equal event probabilities.
hypotheses.alternativeWords: The placebo and aspirin population event probabilities differ.

cases.symbols: \(m_i\) (group event count), \(n_i\) (group size), \(\hat p_i\) (group sample proportion), \(\hat p\) (pooled estimate), \(s_d\) (SE of the difference), \(d\) (observed difference).

steps.title: Define the population difference
steps.words: Use placebo minus aspirin. Equal population event probabilities correspond to a difference of zero.

steps.title: Calculate both sample proportions
steps.words: Each event count is divided by its own group size.

steps.title: Calculate the course pooled proportion
steps.words: Combine event counts and group sizes before taking the fraction. This follows the Session 17 pooled convention.

steps.title: Calculate the pooled binary variance
steps.words: The pooled binary variance is used in both group contributions to the SE.

steps.title: Calculate the difference SE
steps.words: Keep the two group sizes separate inside the square root. The lecture example uses the displayed rounded SE of 0.15 for its interval.

steps.title: Calculate the difference and margin
steps.words: Use the Normal cutoff 1.96 from the infinite-df row, total two-tail 0.05 column. This reproduces the slide’s early-rounded arithmetic.

steps.title: Calculate both endpoints
steps.words: These are absolute differences of event probabilities. Multiply by 100 to express the difference in percentage points.

steps.title: Interpret direction and the zero comparison
steps.words: The interval excludes zero. Retain the placebo minus aspirin order when stating which event probability is higher.

cases.conclusion: The 95% interval for placebo minus aspirin is 0.106 to 0.694, equivalent to 10.60 to 69.40 percentage points. Equal event probabilities are excluded.

cases.title: Non-prescribed stimulant survey
cases.context: Of 500 college-student respondents, 177 answer yes to taking a non-prescribed stimulant in the last year. Determine whether the population proportion differs from one half.
tasks: Construct a 95% CI for the population proportion. Show the estimate, standard error, cutoff, margin, and both bounds.
Determine whether the population proportion differs from 0.5 using the interval. State the hypotheses in symbols and words and interpret the result.

hypotheses.alternativeWords: The population event proportion differs from 0.5.

cases.symbols: \(m\) (event count), \(n\) (sample size), \(\hat p\) (sample event proportion), \(p\) (population event proportion), \(p_0\) (null reference), \(s_{\hat p}\) (estimated SE).

steps.title: State the proportion and hypotheses
steps.words: The null states that the population event proportion is 0.5. The two-sided alternative states that it differs from 0.5.

steps.title: Calculate the sample proportion
steps.words: Divide event count by the total number of observations.

steps.title: Calculate the proportion SE
steps.words: Subtract the proportion from one, multiply, divide by sample size, then take the square root.

steps.title: Select the Normal cutoff
steps.words: Use the infinite-df row of the course two-tail t table. For 95% confidence, the positive cutoff is 1.96.

steps.title: Calculate the margin
steps.words: The margin is in proportion units. Multiply by 100 only when converting the final interpretation to percentage points.

steps.title: Calculate the lower bound
steps.words: Subtract the margin from the observed proportion.

steps.title: Calculate the upper bound
steps.words: Add the same margin to the observed proportion.

steps.title: Compare with the null reference
steps.words: Reject equality with 0.5 at the matching two-sided 0.05 level. The comparison is with the stated reference, not automatically with zero.

cases.conclusion: The 95% CI is 0.3120831 to 0.3959169, or 31.21% to 39.59%. The reference is excluded; the data support a different population proportion.

steps.title: Calculate the proportion SE
steps.words: Subtract the proportion from one, multiply, divide by sample size, then take the square root.

steps.title: Select the Normal cutoff
steps.words: Use the infinite-df row of the course two-tail t table. For 99% confidence, the positive cutoff is 2.5758.

steps.title: Calculate the margin
steps.words: The margin is in proportion units. Multiply by 100 only when converting the final interpretation to percentage points.

steps.title: Calculate the lower bound
steps.words: Subtract the margin from the observed proportion.

steps.title: Calculate the upper bound
steps.words: Add the same margin to the observed proportion.

steps.title: Compare with the null reference
steps.words: Do not reject equality with 0.25 at the matching two-sided 0.01 level. The comparison is with the stated reference, not automatically with zero.

cases.conclusion: The 99% CI is 0.2132276 to 0.3467724, or 21.32% to 34.68%. The reference is included; the data do not reject that population proportion.

cases.title: Event proportions in two treatment groups
cases.context: A study compares two independent groups with an event/no-event outcome for every participant.
tasks: Construct the 95% confidence interval for the difference in population event proportions using the Session 17 pooled standard error. Show both sample proportions, the pooled estimate, variance, SE, margin, and endpoints.
Use the interval to decide whether the event probabilities differ at the matching two-sided 0.05 level. Interpret the direction and distinguish percentage points from a relative reduction.

hypotheses.nullWords: The group1 and group2 populations have equal event probabilities.
hypotheses.alternativeWords: The group1 and group2 population event probabilities differ.

cases.symbols: \(m_i\) (group event count), \(n_i\) (group size), \(\hat p_i\) (group sample proportion), \(\hat p\) (pooled estimate), \(s_d\) (SE of the difference), \(d\) (observed difference).

steps.title: Define the population difference
steps.words: Use group1 minus group2. Equal population event probabilities correspond to a difference of zero.

steps.title: Calculate both sample proportions
steps.words: Each event count is divided by its own group size.

steps.title: Calculate the course pooled proportion
steps.words: Combine event counts and group sizes before taking the fraction. This follows the Session 17 pooled convention.

steps.title: Calculate the pooled binary variance
steps.words: The pooled binary variance is used in both group contributions to the SE.

steps.title: Calculate the difference SE
steps.words: Keep the two group sizes separate inside the square root.

steps.title: Calculate the difference and margin
steps.words: Use the Normal cutoff 1.96 from the infinite-df row, total two-tail 0.05 column.

steps.title: Calculate both endpoints
steps.words: These are absolute differences of event probabilities. Multiply by 100 to express the difference in percentage points.

steps.title: Interpret direction and the zero comparison
steps.words: The interval excludes zero. Retain the group1 minus group2 order when stating which event probability is higher.

cases.conclusion: The 95% interval for group1 minus group2 is 0.02623256 to 0.2737674, equivalent to 2.62 to 27.38 percentage points. Equal event probabilities are excluded.

sampleQuestions.stem: For the bme423 student heart rate study, construct the requested 95% interval using the stated course method. What is its upper endpoint?

sampleQuestions.stem: For the bme423 student heart rate study, construct the requested 95% interval using the stated course method. What is its standard error?
sampleQuestions.why: The standard error is 2.84605 beats/min. Divide the sample SD by the square root of sample size. Keep the standard error available for the margin calculation.
